verdict: OK to lend in Manesar auto OEM supply chain — pursue tier-1/tier-2 vendors with diversified order books and clean receivables; avoid single-OEM, single-plant dependent units and labour-exposed job-work shops.
title: Manesar Cars & Commercial Vehicles (OEM): a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Manesar is a car-assembly town: Maruti's plant builds the Dzire here, and the model has just crossed 3.5 million cumulative units in about 18 years and 9 months [2]. **The OEM is the cash engine; everyone we lend to is a feeder into it — stampings, plastics, wiring, logistics, tooling, job-work labour.** Value sits with the OEM's brand and model mix; our borrowers sit in the conversion margin between steel/commodity input cost and the per-piece price the OEM agrees. Pricing power is thin and reset at annual or model-cycle negotiations, so a vendor's margin is a function of volume per part number, not of price.

## Where cash sits and what has changed
Working capital is the whole game: vendors carry raw material and WIP, then wait on OEM payment terms — **collect the actual receivable days and creditor days from the customer; do not assume.** Capex is tooling and press/moulding capacity tied to a specific model, so it is stranded if the model dies. Locally, the news is mixed: Dzire output pace is quickening [1][2], but the same plant has a history of a labour stir and a temporary production suspension with over 25,000 units of loss reported [3] — that item is undated in the feed, so treat it as background risk, not current fact. Peer results (Q4FY26/Q1FY27) show strong volumes but margin pressure from commodity and freight costs, with price hikes being flagged [4][5][6][7]. **So when a proposal lands, check the share of revenue from one model and one plant; if above roughly half, ask for the second customer and the second part number.**

## The growth opportunity to pursue now
National auto output (IIP NIC 29) is +25.2% YoY and +19.2% Apr-to-date [D], and Haryana GST is running +10.1% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D] — **the local economy is outrunning the country, so lend into the feeder chain, not the headline OEM.** Pursue tier-1 and tier-2 vendors with two or more OEM customers, export-facing suppliers (peers note export-focused OEMs hold margins better [7]), and tooling/logistics providers on annual contracts. Avoid pure labour job-work shops and any unit whose order book is one part number for one model.

## How to grow safely
Bank credit is growing +27.0% YoY against output +19.2%, a +7.8 pp gap [D] — **the system is lending faster than the factory is producing, so our discipline has to be structural, not sentiment.** Structure: cash-flow backed working capital limits sized to the drawing cycle, not to peak turnover; monthly stock-and-receivable statements; escrow of OEM receivables where the OEM pays into a designated account. Take every month: stock statement, debtor ageing by OEM, GST returns, and a plant-visit note. **If the debtor ageing shows one OEM above the agreed share, cut the limit before renewing.**

## Early-warning signs
- Monthly stock/receivable statement (monthly): receivable days stretch beyond the agreed band -> freeze enhancement and reprice.
- GST returns (monthly): turnover falls two months running -> ask for the order book and visit the plant.
- OEM payment advice (monthly): payment routed outside the escrow -> treat as a red flag and seek explanation in writing.
- Plant visit (quarterly): idle presses or reduced shifts -> reassess limit and seek a second-customer plan.
- Labour/news watch (weekly): any strike or suspension report at the Manesar plant [3] -> pause new sanctions in single-OEM vendors.
